text: Let's take a look at a verse from the
Bible that will tell you if your
translation of the Bible is prioritizing
dogma over data. Hey everybody, I'm Dan
McClellan. I'm a scholar of the Bible
and religion, and we're going to look at
Genesis 2:19, which is an otherwise
rather uneventful verse. But here it is
from the updated edition of the New
Revised Standard Version. So, out of the
ground, the Lord God formed every animal
of the field and every bird of the air
and brought them to the man to see what
he would call them, and whatever the man
called every living creature, that was
its name. This is a fine translation of
the Hebrew. There's nothing wrong here.
However,
this creates a contradiction between the
two different creation accounts because
this places the creation of all the
animals after the creation of the human.
But in Genesis 1, all the animals are
created before the creation of the
human. And so, if you presuppose the
univocality of the text and you refuse
to accept contradictions in the text,
you've got a problem here. You need to
find a way to try to gloss over the fact
that this contradicts Genesis 1. And
what some translations have done to try
to accomplish that is they've rendered
the first verb in the pluperfect. And
so, instead of "So out of the ground the
Lord God formed every animal of the
field," some translations will render
"the Lord God had formed every animal of
the field," making it sound like the
narrator is bringing up something that
actually happened earlier. And the
biggest translations that I can think of
that do this are the NIV, the ESV, the
LSB, the Legacy Standard Bible, which is
MacArthur's revision of the NASB. But
the NASB doesn't do it. The LSB actually
revises this translation error into
their translation. Those three
translations very clearly put dogma over
data. And if you look at their
backgrounds and their translation
philosophies, they all assert belief in
the inspiration and the inerrancy of the
text. And so, this is an example of
where people will overrule what's
actually in the text in order to impose
their dogmas upon it and tell the text
what it is and is not allowed to say.
Now, really what this comes down to is a
single Hebrew word. This is the Hebrew
of this passage, and in the red box,
you've got vayyitser. And that comes
from the verbal root yatsar, which means
to fashion, to form, to create. And it's
in a form known as the wayyiqtol. And
this is past time narrative sequence.
It's where you say this happened, then
this happened, then this happened, then
this happened. And the wayyiqtol usually
is translated in the perfect, so just
the simple past. And that's how it
should be translated here.
It is not impossible to translate it as
a pluperfect, but it is very rare, and
certain criteria have to be met for the
case for a pluperfect rendering to be
plausible. And you can find those
criteria in this book from 1994,
Biblical Hebrew and Discourse
Linguistics. And Randall Booth has a
paper in here, Methodological Collision
Between Source Criticism and Discourse
Analysis, The Problem of Unmarked
Temporal Overlay and the Pluperfect
{slash} Non-Sequential Wayyiqtol. And
Booth basically argues that there are
three criteria that have to be met in
order to plausibly render a wayyiqtol as
a pluperfect. And Booth points out those
criteria are not met for Genesis 2:19.
It cannot be interpreted as a
pluperfect. The very next year, in an
evangelical journal called the Tyndale
Bulletin, C. John Collins published The
Wayyiqtol as Pluperfect: When and Why,
and rejects Booth's argument, and
concludes that Genesis 2:19 can be
rendered as a pluperfect. And the entire
argument is found within this red box on
this page and this red box on this page.
And it can be summed up very easily.
Collins argues that we should assume
that Genesis 1
harmonizes with Genesis 2.
If not because we imagine that that's
what one single author originally
composed, at the very least, we must
conclude that the editor who brought
them together wanted us to read them as
a single harmonious narrative.
Now, the case for that is not very easy
to make. And Collins uses chiasmus,
which has long been rejected by scholars
as something that can really strongly
indicates the intent and the motivations
of the authors or editors. More than
anything else, it indicates the
creativity of the modern reader. But the
point I'm trying to make is that
Collins' entire case is basically
begging the question because if you just
isolate Genesis 2:19 within its
immediate context, within the sense unit
of which it is a part and in which it is
embedded, it simply does not meet the
criteria, even according to Collins' own
argument. For Collins' argument to work,
you must expand the scope and include
Genesis 1, which is a separate sense
unit. And then you must assume that it
is intended to harmonize with Genesis 2.
And that's where it's begging the
question because the whole point of
writing this paper, the only reason
Collins even wrote this paper is because
he wants to defend the univocality of
the text. He wants to defend a
pluperfect interpretation of this verb
the beginning of Genesis 2:19 because
that resolves the contradiction. And the
argument that allows him to resolve the
contradiction is basically, well, we
should understand it to not be
contradicting. And if it's not
contradicting, then the pluperfect
reading is correct. And it's problematic
for a number of other reasons, but in
the most simple and basic terms, Collins
is basically presupposing the conclusion
in the premise. And the argument that is
made for including that conclusion in
the premise is not a very strong one. It
has been addressed many times by
critical scholars in the past. So, the
verb at the beginning of Genesis 2:19
cannot plausibly be interpreted as a
pluperfect, which is why the
overwhelming majority of translations do
not translate it that way. And the only
ones that do are very dogmatic
translations like the NIV, like the ESV,
like the LSB that put dogma over data.
And this verse cannot tell you if your
translation is a good one, but if your
translation renders this in the
pluperfect, this verse can tell you that
it is a bad one. And if it's for this
